transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-26
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Evan Park (Redwood Eng); Sofia Martinez (Aurora Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (Aurora Infra), Grace Chen (Aurora PM), Noah Diaz (Aurora Data Eng)

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): Hey folks, thanks for hopping on — quick check-in on caching work, specifically prefix and KV cache hit rates. I think we have about 40 mins. Sofia, want to kick off with any updates on your side?

[00:18] Sofia (Aurora): Yeah thanks Jordan. Nothing huge changed this week, we did collect another 48 hours of prod-like traffic as you asked, attached to the sheet. We still see pretty fragmented prompt patterns — clinicians vary templates a lot — so curious about the fuzzy matching numbers you mentioned last week.

[00:35] Priya (Redwood): Great, we ran two clusters of experiments: exact-prefix matching and then a normalization pass (whitespace, small token-level edits, and canonicalization of certain placeholders). Exact-prefix steady state hit was roughly 34-38% depending on the routing and batch size. With normalization we saw hits jump to about 58-64% on the sampled traces. Those are across 2M warm keys in the KV cache.

[01:05] Liam (Aurora): That's higher than I expected for normalization — how aggressive is the normalization? I worry about over-normalizing and incorrectly conflating different prompts.

[01:20] Evan (Redwood): Good question. Our normalization was conservative: lowercasing, trimming multi-space, normalizing dates/times to tokens, and collapse of clinician name placeholders like [DOC_NAME]. We didn't rewrite clinical terms. The fuzzy match window used Levenshtein threshold tuned to prefer exact matches; we only fall back to fuzzy if exact misses for >2 similar tokens. So risk of conflation is low but not zero.

[01:50] Grace (Aurora): Can you share concrete examples where normalization helped? We want to see before/after so our clinicians can evaluate correctness.

[02:05] Priya (Redwood): Sure — I'll attach a 20-row sample in the follow-up. Example: "Generate a patient summary for John Doe born 12/05/1980" vs "generate patient summary - John D., b. 12 May 1980" — normalization hits both to same canonical prefix and uses cached KV to skip model forward pass.

[02:30] Sofia (Aurora): Ok, that makes sense. What about prompt reuse beyond prefix — we have partial reuse where the system appends different labs each time; can KV help there?

[02:48] Priya: We support partial KV reuse via prefix + suffix segmentation. If the variable suffix (like lab table) is long, KV cache stores the decoder KV up to the prefix and then we warm the decoder with that cache, reducing token cost for generation. For very long suffixes we don't get cache hits but we still save generation steps if the decoded prefix is reused.

[03:12] Noah (Aurora): In our traces the free-text summary body changes 70% of the time but the intro/structured header is highly stable. So it sounds promising. Do you have numbers for average token savings when prefix is cached?

[03:25] Evan: On our samples, when the prefix hits the KV cache, we save 20-40% of model compute depending on model and prefix length — e.g., for a 512-token prefix against a 4k context model the effective per-call token compute dropped by ~28%.

[03:50] Liam: How about tail latency? Does fetching from KV add any latency versus full forward?

[04:00] Priya: KV fetch is fast — in-memory hot path adds ~5-12ms additional latency, but avoids a full transformer forward which is hundreds of ms depending on tokens. Net latency for a popular path is typically lower. We do have cold-key lookups that can add slightly more if S3-backed tiering is used.

[04:28] Sofia: You mentioned hit rates were with 2M keys. We have about 10M unique prompts over a month. Does hit rate scale down as key space grows?

[04:40] Evan: There's a curve — with more keys, exact-match density drops. Normalization and prefix canonicalization help a lot. We also saw that most hit volume comes from a long tail: the top 200k prefixes account for ~45% of hits in our sample. So if you focus on warm starters (top-K caching) you can get disproportionate wins.

[05:05] Grace: That suggests we should consider an eviction/priority policy that pins the top X prefixes. Is that supported?

[05:12] Priya: Yes — we support LRU, LFU, and pinned keys for reserved warm sets. For Dedicated we can give a pinned heap and guarantee residency. For hosted we can approximate pinning with priority refresh.

[05:35] Sofia: We are interested in Dedicated later in the POC but for now hosted is easier. Are there cost calculations to show when Dedicated makes sense for caching?

[05:47] Jordan: We have a cost model template. Priya, can you summarize the delta?

[05:55] Priya: Short answer: when your warm-hit rate is high enough that token savings pay for reserved capacity plus the pinning overhead. In rough numbers from our model, with your traffic profile if sustained warm hit >45% and average request size >600 prompt tokens, Dedicated reserved capacity starts to pay off versus pure hosted per-token pricing. We'll update the sheet with the new observed hit rates.

[06:23] Sofia: Perfect. On the metrics side, can you annotate the telemetry so we can see per-route hit rates and per-user breakdowns? We want to prove we aren't conflating different clinicians.

[06:35] Evan: We can emit per-route, per-customer, and prefix-cluster telemetry. The PII-sensitive fields are hashed; we can do session-level aggregation so you can spot if a single clinician dominates a prefix cluster.

[06:55] Liam: Which fields are hashed? We need to ensure names are not in logs for compliance.

[07:03] Priya: Names and raw patient identifiers are hashed; we keep structural tokens like [DATE], [LAB_TABLE] as placeholders. Audit logs show hits/misses but not raw PII. We can share SOC-2 docs and the masking scheme.

[07:20] Sofia: Please do. Also, how are you measuring fuzzy-match false positives?

[07:26] Evan: We randomly sample fuzzy-match events and run an automated similarity score plus a manual audit for edge cases. In our sample of 1k fuzzy matches, manual review flagged ~1.2% as problematic where the canonicalization removed clinically-relevant differences. We're tuning to reduce that.

[07:50] Grace: What about prompt templating on our side — we could standardize clinician templates to increase hit rates. Is there tooling to help generate canonical templates?

[08:02] Priya: We have a small toolkit and some best-practice docs: suggest canonical placeholders, move variable tables to attachments rather than inline, and use stable header tokens. If you can reduce syntactic variance by 20-30% we see large hit-rate improvements. We'll share the doc link in the follow-up.

[08:23] Sofia: We'll try to prototype one clinical template next week.

[08:30] Noah: Quick infra question: if we push cached keys from our side (pre-warm), what's the API?

[08:37] Evan: There's a REST prewarm endpoint you can call with prefix keys; for Dedicated we also support a bulk sync to the node-local store. Pre-warm costs are modest for hosted but we can give credits as part of the pilot.

[08:55] Liam: Regarding evictions, if we pin keys does that affect autoscaling?

[09:02] Priya: If you're pinned, we reserve memory; autoscaling can still add nodes but the pinned set is replicated across nodes, so you'll need the dedicated heap size factored into instance sizing. We'll provide a recommended instance footprint.

[09:20] Grace: Can we talk about specific numbers we saw in last week's run? I looked at the shared CSV and there were columns for attempts, exact_hits, fuzzy_hits, miss. Can someone walk through the top-line?

[09:35] Priya: Sure — from the 48h run: total requests 82,400. Exact hits: 28,220 (~34.2%). Fuzzy normalized hits: 16,970 (~20.6%). Misses: ~37,210 (~45.2%). After we applied a top-K pin of 250k warm keys in a follow-up run, exact+fuzzy combined rose to ~61.8% on the same traffic slice.

[10:05] Sofia: That's promising. Were those numbers from the same time window? I'm asking because our traffic spikes at 02:00 UTC when US clinicians batch notes.

[10:15] Evan: Yes same window; we also looked at spike windows and the hit rate dips by ~8-10% during bursts because new prompts arrive. Pinning helps with that.

[10:35] Jordan: Let's discuss risk: false positive fuzzy hits could cause incorrect outputs. What's the mitigation?

[10:42] Priya: We have a fallback policy: when fuzzy match is used we increase conservatism — we can attach a confidence flag and optionally re-run the model on a full pass if downstream safety checks fail. Also you can disable fuzzy in high-risk routes.

[11:00] Grace: For example, discharge summaries are high risk; we want to avoid fuzzy there. Others like patient intake notes are lower risk.

[11:08] Sofia: Agreed. We'll flag high-risk routes in the prompt list.

[11:15] Noah: On the prompt reuse strategy, what about template-level caching vs token-level?

[11:20] Evan: Template-level caching (i.e., whole prefix) gives the best savings. Token-level partial reuse via KV is more flexible but lower hit density. Our suggestion: standardize templates for high-value routes and allow token-level for secondary routes.

[11:36] Priya: Also worth noting: the model choice matters. Larger models have more KV/state memory and can benefit more from caching for long sequences; quantized smaller models behave differently with cache pressure. We'll note model-specific guidance in the README.

[11:55] Sofia: One procedural ask — can you provide an anonymized sample of fuzzy false positives so our clinicians can audit?

[12:02] Priya: Yes we'll include 25 examples in the follow-up: both true positives and false positives with explanations.

[12:12] Jordan: Great. Let's roll into next steps and timeline. We've captured a few already but want to be explicit.

[12:20] Priya: Action items recap — Redwood: scale KV benchmark to 4M keys and run the top-K pinning test; share full CSV and dashboard link. Aurora: share canonical prompt families and mark high-risk routes. Redwood to update cost model with new hit rates. Then we'll plan a longer dedicated perf run (could be private/Dedicated) if those metrics look good.

[12:48] Sofia: One more—on telemetry can you break down hits by clinician role? We think nurses vs physicians use templates differently.

[12:56] Evan: We can do aggregated role buckets if you provide role mapping for user ids — hashed of course.

[13:10] Jordan: Anything else?

[13:15] Grace: Not from me. This was helpful. Please send the sample rows and the updated cost sheet.

[13:22] Sofia: Thanks all.

[13:25] Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with artifacts.

[13:30] (meeting ends)

Notes: Links / artifacts mentioned: shared CSV (drive link), cost-model sheet (redacted link), normalization best-practices doc (link), sample fuzzy-match audit (attached in follow-up).

End of transcript.
